title: SDK first 100 requests — empiric matrix and quick validation runbook
content:
Objective:
Run a lightweight, repeatable validation of a new SDK quickstart by sending the first 100 real-ish requests and capturing observability & cost signals. This is a pragmatic bridge between a code-level smoke test and a small-scale field test — good for PR signoff and early customer demos.

Why this helps (context):
- Many quickstarts pass unit tests but fail to reveal real-world pain: cold KV cache, first-token latency, telemetry tags missing, or bad error messages.
- Doing a controlled run of the first 100 requests surfaces: SDK init overhead, default batching behavior, retry surface, and how prompt scaffolding impacts latency/cost.
- The experiment is cheap, reproducible, and yields data useful for both SDK ergonomics and product telemetry requirements.

High-level experiment design (empiric matrix):
We vary three axes (minimal combinatorics to keep runs quick):
- Runtime surface: local dev (CLI devserver) | CI (hermetic Docker) | playground (hosted sandbox)
- Workload type: chat-completion (multi-turn) | single-shot generation (templated) | embedding call (small)
- Network conditions: ideal (local LAN) | 90ms RTT sim | 250ms RTT sim + 1% loss

For each run capture these signals (minimum):
- Request-level: timestamp, route/model, input token count, response token count, request duration (ms), time-to-first-byte (ms), HTTP status, retry count
- SDK-level: cold init time (ms), connection setup (ms), telemetry tags emitted (boolean list), batching size observed (if any), cache hit/miss per-prefix
- Cost: estimated token cost (per Redwood pricing), number of backend model calls (if routing to fallback counted), approximate GPU-seconds (if available)

Run procedure (quickstart mode):
1) Seed: pick three representative prompts (concise, medium, long). Document them in the run artifacts folder.
2) Env: use two SDK configurations — default (out-of-the-box) and adjusted (batching disabled, smaller max_tokens).
3) Warmup: for the local and CI runs, do 5 warmup requests (not counted) to populate ephemeral caches.
4) Execute: run 100 sequential requests with 200–500ms inter-request jitter to simulate a developer demo cadence.
5) Record: dump raw telemetry JSON per-request and an aggregated CSV (one row per request).
6) Post-process: compute P50/P95 latency, first-byte percentiles, cost per 1k tokens, failure rate, and a small qualitative note for any unusual error.

Acceptance criteria (quick checks for PR reviewers):
- Mean init time < 250ms (comment: init includes auth + connection handshake)
- P95 latency (first byte) < 600ms under ideal conditions for single-shot small prompts
- No uncaught exceptions in SDK logs for any of the 100 requests
- All telemetry events contain the route and environment tag (dev|ci|playground)
- Error rate <= 2% (transient 5xx or timeouts allowed but flagged)

Quick validation checklist for engineers (copyable into PR template):
- [ ] Attach run artifact: raw-requests.json + aggregated.csv
- [ ] Link to test prompts used
- [ ] Confirm run environment and SDK version
- [ ] Summarize top 3 regressions or surprises (if any)
- [ ] If failure, paste failing request ID and error stack

Common failure modes & mitigation notes (observed in earlier pilots):
- Long auth token exchange: ensure token cache TTLs set and refresh path tested in CI (mitigation: reuse token pre-run).
- Large default max_tokens causing high P95: lower demo max_tokens to 128 for quickstarts.
- Invisible telemetry: telemetry not flushed before process exit — add sync/flush hook in CLI quickstart.
- Batching surprises: local dev bundling large batches when not expected (set batching=0 for demo).

Artifacts to keep after a run (minimum):
- raw-requests.json (list of per-request telemetry blobs)
- aggregated.csv (one row per request, CSV-friendly columns)
- prompts.txt
- run-notes.md (short narrative of anomalies and config used)

How this feeds other workstreams:
- SDK UX: use telemetry gaps found here to add guardrails (e.g., automatic flush, better init progress).
- Product: provide a short table for the quickstart page with expected P95 under ideal net and recommended demo knobs.
- QA/Automation: convert the empiric matrix into a small CI job that runs weekly against the quickstart branch to detect regressions.

Next steps (owner: Riley Chen):
- Convert this document into a templated test script (bash + node) that can be run with two flags: --env=(local|ci|playground) and --config=(default|demo). Target: prototype by 2025-11-17.
- Hook the script to a PR checklist (Linear ticket above).
- Share with Solutions Eng and Documentation for feedback the week after the prototype.

Open questions (for triage):
- Which telemetry IDs are authoritative for correlating SDK telemetry with backend traces? (ping infra/reliability)
- Do we want to capture model warm-start metrics (cold vs hot KV cache) separately?

Notes to self: keep the run artifacts small — limit raw-requests.json to first 1000 lines for storage retention policy. Make sure to redact any customer data in saved prompts.

Appendix — sample run summary (example output format):
- run_id: rwd-demo-20251103-01
- env: local
- sdk_version: v0.9.3-beta
- prompts: [short.txt, medium.txt, long.txt]
- results_highlights: P50=82ms, P95=432ms, error_rate=0.0%, avg_tokens_in=18, avg_tokens_out=42

End.
